questions.q: A learner's family invites the technician to a birthday party at their home. Which principle should guide the answer?
options: Avoid a multiple relationship; tell the supervisor
Attend to build rapport with the family outside of sessions
Attend but do not bring a gift
Ask the learner whether you should come
questions.explain: Attending social events with a client's family can create a multiple relationship that blurs professional boundaries. The ethics code for technicians asks them to avoid such relationships and to involve the supervisor when one arises.

questions.q: Which action best shows treating a learner with dignity?
options: Talking about the learner's behavior loudly in the waiting room
Offering choices and privacy during care routines
Using a nickname the learner dislikes
Rushing through toileting in a hallway
questions.explain: Dignity includes respecting choices and privacy, especially during personal care. Discussing a learner in public spaces or using unwanted names fails to treat the learner with respect.

questions.q: A technician is asked to run a procedure they have never been trained on. What should they do?
options: Try it and learn from any mistakes along the way with the learner
Watch an online video and start
Tell the supervisor and get trained first
Ask the learner to show how it works
questions.explain: Technicians provide services only after showing competence. When a new procedure comes up, they ask for training from the supervisor, which may include instructions, modeling, rehearsal and feedback.

questions.q: A technician's supervisor leaves the company, and no new supervisor is assigned. What follows?
options: Services can continue as usual for six months while the company looks
The technician can supervise themselves
A teacher can sign the supervision form
No RBT services until a qualified supervisor is in place
questions.explain: Technicians practice only under ongoing supervision by someone who meets the board's requirements. Without a qualified supervisor, they cannot deliver services as RBTs. The organization must arrange new supervision.

questions.q: Which is part of effective supervision for a technician?
options: Training with feedback and observation of sessions
Occasional emails with no observation of the technician at work
Supervision only when problems occur
A yearly written test
questions.explain: Effective supervision uses behavioral skills training (instructions, modeling, rehearsal and feedback) and direct observation of the technician working with clients. Supervision is ongoing, not only when there is a problem.

questions.q: A supervisor gives corrective feedback after observing a session. What is the most professional response?
options: Explain in detail why the feedback is wrong for that learner
Listen, clarify and apply the feedback
Stop working with that learner
Ask another supervisor for a different opinion
questions.explain: Accepting feedback and applying it is part of the professional skills expected of technicians. Asking clarifying questions is helpful. Arguing, shopping for other opinions or withdrawing from a case are not constructive.

questions.q: A technician wants to take a photo of a learner's great work to share with friends. What does confidentiality require?
options: Share it if the learner's face is not shown and names are visible
Share it only with close friends
Share nothing that identifies a client outside the rules
Share it if the learner agrees verbally
questions.explain: Client information, including photos and work samples, is confidential. It is collected, stored and shared only as the workplace's policies and the law allow, usually with written consent. Partial hiding or a verbal okay from a learner is not enough.

questions.q: Where should printed data sheets with client names be kept after a session?
options: In the technician's car until the weekend, in a closed bag
On the clinic's front desk
In a personal folder at home
In the secure place the workplace sets
questions.explain: Records that identify clients must be stored securely as required by workplace policies and privacy laws. Leaving them in cars, public areas or at home risks unauthorized disclosure.

questions.q: A technician posts on social media that their company "cures autism." What is the problem?
options: It misrepresents the field and its outcomes
Nothing is wrong, because it is posted on a personal account
It is fine if the company approves
The post should include a client's name for proof
questions.explain: Public statements, including on social media, must not misrepresent the field, outcomes or credentials. Claiming a cure is false. Adding a client's name would also break confidentiality.

questions.q: Which statement about credentials is accurate in a public profile?
options: Calling oneself a behavior analyst because one works in ABA
The credential exactly as held, while active
Keeping the credential listed after it expires
Adding a credential that is in progress
questions.explain: Technicians must represent their credentials accurately. A technician is not a behavior analyst, an expired credential cannot be displayed as current, and a credential in progress is not yet held.

questions.q: A technician is offered the chance to babysit for a current client's family on weekends. What is the concern?
options: There is no concern as long as the babysitting hours are paid
It is fine if the supervisor is not told
A multiple relationship that risks harm
It is required to build rapport
questions.explain: Taking a second role with a client's family, such as babysitting, is a multiple relationship. It risks conflicts of interest and harm to the client. Such roles are avoided, and any that arise are discussed with the supervisor.

questions.q: A technician discovers that a new client is the child of a close friend. What should happen?
options: Continue the case and give the friend extra updates each week
Keep quiet to avoid awkwardness
Ask the friend to sign a waiver
Tell the supervisor so the risk is handled
questions.explain: Existing personal relationships with a client's family create a multiple relationship. The technician informs the supervisor promptly, who can reduce the risk, for example by assigning another technician.

questions.q: At the end of services, a family offers the technician an expensive watch. What should they do?
options: Decline politely, as the gift rules require
Accept it because services are ending and the gift is a thank you
Accept it and share it with the team
Accept it if the family insists twice
questions.explain: The ethics code for technicians limits gifts to items of small monetary value and the workplace may be stricter. An expensive gift crosses that line whatever the timing. A kind refusal protects the professional relationship.

questions.q: A learner draws a picture for the technician as a thank you. What is a reasonable response?
options: Refuse it because every gift from a family is banned
Accept it if workplace policy allows
Ask for a more useful gift
Sell it
questions.explain: Small tokens of appreciation with little monetary value, like a drawing, are generally within the gift rules of the ethics code. The technician still follows the employer's policy, which may be stricter.

questions.q: During a team meeting, a caregiver disagrees with the technician's account of a session. What shows good interpersonal skills?
options: Defend the account until the caregiver agrees with every detail
Leave the meeting
Listen, acknowledge and refer plan questions to the supervisor
Change the data to match the caregiver's view
questions.explain: Active listening, respect and collaboration are expected professional skills. The technician can share objective data and refer decisions to the supervisor. Changing data to end a disagreement would be falsification.

questions.q: A technician realizes they hold a bias about a family's cultural practices. What reflects cultural humility?
options: Ignore it because it does not affect data
Ask to be removed from every case of that culture
Teach the family to adopt the technician's own practices at home
Reflect, learn the family's values, raise it in supervision
questions.explain: Cultural humility involves ongoing self-reflection, learning about each family's values, and raising biases in supervision so services stay respectful and effective. Ignoring a bias or imposing one's own practices does not serve the client.

questions.q: A caregiver texts the technician late at night with several questions about the treatment plan. What is the most professional response?
options: Answer each question in detail right away
Ignore every message from the caregiver
Give an opinion on whether the plan works
Refer plan questions to the supervisor in work hours
questions.explain: Professional boundaries call for communication through the agreed channels and hours, and questions about the plan belong to the supervisor who designed it. Ignoring the family harms the relationship, and detailed answers or opinions about the plan go beyond the technician's role.

questions.q: A family asks that no sessions be scheduled during a religious holiday the technician has never heard of. What reflects cultural humility?
options: Ask the family about it and inform the supervisor
Keep the usual schedule because data matter most
Decide alone which holidays are important enough
Tell the family the request is not standard
questions.explain: Cultural humility means learning from the family about what matters to them, respecting it, and involving the supervisor in any change to the schedule. Overriding the request, judging which holidays count or calling it nonstandard puts the technician's own view above the family's values.

questions.q: A technician's cousin enrolls her child at the clinic, and the technician is assigned to the case. What should the technician do?
options: Accept the case since they already know the child
Tell the supervisor about the relationship before starting
Work with the child but keep it from the team
Ask the cousin to keep the relationship private
questions.explain: A family tie with a client is a multiple relationship that can affect objectivity. The technician discloses it to the supervisor before services start so the case can be reassigned or managed. Hiding it or relying on familiarity creates exactly the conflict the code seeks to avoid.
